rationale: A is stronger because its first-wave mitigations include OS-enforced filesystem isolation, protected policy configuration, and explicit treatment of subprocesses as untrusted, whereas B postpones OS sandboxing and relies initially on application-level path checks that cannot constrain arbitrary spawned commands or package scripts. Both responses overstate command allowlists and secret-pattern redaction—nominally safe commands such as test runners and package managers can execute arbitrary project code—but A more realistically bounds damage if the model is fully compromised. B also makes unsupported claims about prompt tagging reducing risk “by an order of magnitude,” understates egress-control complexity, and incorrectly suggests signed model responses eliminate a compromised-backend trust boundary. A therefore has the sounder prioritization and more defensible threat reasoning despite some implementation caveats.
